node.text: Nerd’s Eye View: LA Auto Show 2025
Mark read

As I was walking into the 2025 LA Auto Show around six months ago, I came across Larry Chen’s camera car before the sea of food trucks and a slew of EVs. It actually forebode a bit the variety of vehicles at the show with various appendages and big power.

This suction cup is the beefiest I’ve ever seen. At least I think it’s a suction cup and not a mount that’s just drilled through the hood. The clamp has a TUV sticker on it, so it’s good enough for the Germans.
That mounts have to be strong to support this rig. The camera mount has a bunch of through-shaft dampers and weights to keep the camera steady while the car is bouncing around.
Out by the food trucks, Rivian had a couple of their vans on display and a couple rows of cars for test rides.
I had this yummy combo for breakfast.

Get ready for the incoming wave of autonomous vehicles. Tensor had a car on display to showcase their Level 4 autonomy system. The system uses a bunch of cameras and a lidar unit on the roof to keep from hitting things.
Flying cars has been a dream of humanity for a half century. If you look back at Popular Mechanics magazine, they’ve been showing flying cars from the 1960’s.
For things that fly, weight is everything. So, you can see that carbon fiber is used everywhere. The modern flying cars are EVs. I’m guessing those heat sinks are for cooling the motors or inverters.
Scout made a splash at the show this year. With this being a show car, it had a lot of non-production intent parts. At least that’s what I think I overheard….
I’m not exactly sure how to read this “100 x kPa / psi” label. Show car things I guess.
Maybe it’s just me, but the rear anti-roll bar looks really small to me. I guess it’s some compromise between on-road handling and off-road articulation.
It’s been a long time since I looked at an IndyCar up close. A lot has changed.
IndyCar went with the aero screen instead of the halo used on Formula 1 cars. I imagine the teams use side intake plates with different opening areas depending on the cooling needs.

It’s been a while since I kept up with IndyCar powertrain tech. It’s clearly twin-turbo with the wastegate dumps separated from the turbine outlet flow. The hot air coming off the heat exchangers dumps out those louvers. It’s a bit hard to see, but just outboard of all that hot airflow is the cooling air to the rear brake ducts. Oh yeah, IndyCar uses a hybrid powertrain now.

I find it slightly amusing that open wheel race cars are using 15” wheels and 20” wheels are common on street cars. IndyCar uses magnesium wheels, but they have talked about switching to aluminum for cost reduction.

It looks like the front brake ducts are grabbing air coming off the bottom side of the front wing. There is a lot of range of adjustment for the front wing judging by the length of the slot next to the adjuster.
Speaking of street cars with big wheels, the Hyundai Elantra N comes with 19” wheels to fit over a big set of brakes.
If you want an even quicker Hyundai, the IONIQ 6N was on display.
I’m surprised the rear underbody aero wasn’t more aggressive being a ‘N’ car.
Hyundai had this soccer shooting simulator in prep for the World Cup.
Toyota crammed a modern engine into an old chassis giving it modern power and cleaner emissions to boot. It’s a resto-mod I guess? They called it the Turbo Trail Cruiser.
The twin turbo V6 out of the Tundra did fit into the old engine bay. I imagine it’s way more fun than the old engine and probably better mpg too.
I never could get the toy out of these machines.
I don’t really understand why there is an ‘truck’ racing series in addition to stock cars, but I’m sure it’s still fun.
Some old school cowl induction.
That’s a big diameter fuel line. At first, I thought it was a little sketchy that it ran through the cabin, but that’s probably the safest place for it being well-protected inside the cage structure.
That’s a lot of tire rubber caught on the various structures underneath the body.
I don’t really keep up with the exotic cars, but this is a cool looking Alfa Romeo 33 Stradale.

I didn’t look to hard, but there doesn’t seem to be a ton of heat exchanger exhaust air venting; it’s all very subtle. There’s a little slot at the base of the windshield which I’d guess is to vent hot air out of the engine bay. There’s another slot in the carbon fiber panel at the rear of the decklid. I’m sure there’s more exhaust flow area between the rear taillights, but I didn’t look closely. And there appear to be slots in the rear panel, between the red panel and the carbon fiber panel holding the taillight.
For a million dollar car, I wouldn’t be happy with the swirl marks on the clear panels. I imagine they are a polycarbonate and not glass.
Jeep had these big ramps to drive their cars on scare passengers. Ford had one too.

Volvo had this cool display showing the different types of materials used to make a unibody frame. The high-strength stuff where needed for stiffness and crash protection, the cheaper stuff where it’s just for looks.
Everyone is making an off-road rig out of everything. Volvo made one out of their EX30. My bro-in-law has the street EX30 in the dual-motor performance trim. It’s very quick.
Nissan had this built 400Z on a lifted platform. It has a good-looking brake package.
It’s nice that Nismo offers quality suspension bits that remove all the factory squishy rubber chunks. I’m not quite sure what’s going on with that partial shiny disk inside the wheel.
It’s not good practice to go from a larger diameter downpipe to a smaller diameter mid-pipe. I’m just going to guess, show car things.
This exhaust is interesting too. I don’t understand why each side goes from a single pipe, splits into two, and recombines into one to the exhaust tip.
Hyundai had more World Cup advertising going on.
I’m not a fan of retracting door handles; I first ran into them many LA Auto Shows ago on the Jaguar I-Pace. There’s a little IONIQ 9 label that gets hidden when the handle disappears.
Autonomous cars are coming and this IONIQ 5 is outfitted with an extra sensor package for Waymo.
VW had this modified Golf on display. It allows a person to drive it with only hand controls.

I wish I had gotten a closer look at the controls. I would assume the lower control next to the center console is the throttle and brake. There’s some control lever to the lower left of the steering wheel; maybe it’s for an old school foot-actuated parking brake?
I didn’t spend much time looking around the VW booth because I got distracted by this section with all the adults playing.
VW provided these little car kits you built and could race down the ramps.
We all had fun decorating out vehicles.
Genesis is launching this ‘Magma’ vehicle line. My decorated car has the right color on it along with a similar Dr. Evil eye expression.
I stopped by the Subaru booth to pet a few dogs.

The trunk for the C8 Corvette is pretty large. I think it’s a product requirement to be able to fit a set of golf clubs in a Vette. It’s got a pretty good seal around the opening which should keep hot air from the engine bay from leaking into the trunk.

The mounts for the struts to hold open the rear hatch are pretty beefy. I haven’t kept up with all the tech on the Z06, but this one has electronically adjustable dampers judging by the wire harness going into the top of the damper. Beefy braces span the engine bay going from the rear shock mounting locations to the passenger compartment bulkhead.
A lot of power means a lot of exhaust heat. The headers are fully insulated. The chassis brace makes a convenient mounting point for whatever that hose is.
The Z06 has large side scoops ramming air through heat exchangers. There was an issue apparently where spilled gasoline got sucked through the side scoop, hit the hot header, and started a fire.
The ZR1X is a whole different beast with a hybrid powertrain attached to the twin-turbo V8. I think it’s the quickest 0-60mph car you can buy.

With the heat created by 1,250hp, a lot of heat exchanger surface area and airflow is required to keep everything cool. I’m assuming the opening between the center and side heat exchangers are for cooling the front brakes.
The ZR1X has an extra air scoop above the main scoop that the Z06 does not have.

I’m a bit surprised there’s not much in the way of a diffuser, but maybe they needed the area for excavating hot air out of the engine bay. As for the exhaust tips, I would have preferred Chevy just extended the real metal tips instead of having the fake chrome ones.
A lot of the rear bumper surface area is for exhausting hot air.
Half of the front hood is cut open to exhaust the hot air out of the front heat exchangers.
This VW bus has all manner of cameras, radar, and I’m assuming LIDAR to enable autonomous driving.
Man…. The Raptor has been around 15 years already. I’m getting old.
The rear is a mini storage center with a jack, spare fluids, spare tires, a driveshaft, and probably a few other things.
This tubular structure beefs up the structure. I imagine it helps keep the chassis from bending in half going over jumps.
A big skid plate helps protect the front of the truck, though a section is cut open for airflow. The exhaust dumps out towards the ground in the middle of the truck.
Porsche hasn’t had a both since COVID, so Porsche Downtown LA had some cars on display.

The 992 generation of 911 got smarter and put the intercoolers right at the rear deck air inlet instead of in the corners of the car. I do wonder how many leaves and things end up on the intercoolers and how easy it would be to suck everything out.

The other smarter thing Porsche did on the higher-end 992s is have the intercooler air dump right out the middle of the car. This makes a very direct airflow path for the external cooling air to go into and out of the intercoolers.
You’ve heard me say it before, that I despise the fake exhaust tips in the rear bumper. That looks like a little bit of weld spatter around the tips in the muffler.
On the way out of the show, I grabbed a burger and fries for the road.

There’s a few trends I have observed the last couple of years. More off-road looking vehicles which are actually better for dealing with our crappy roads with massive potholes. More electrification and tools to allow people to play on their phones instead of driving. Finally, the horsepower of vehicles keeps on going up, whether they be gas, EV, or hybrid. You can go buy a 4-door sedan or a 2-door sportscar that will run 8s in the quarter mile while meeting all modern emissions; I remember back in the day when a car doing 0-60 in the 8’s was considered decently quick. What a time to be alive.
